newsitem.title: GERMANY: SWIMMING-ROLPH DENIED EUROPEAN RECORD, BRITISH TEAM TO APPEAL.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-ROLPH DENIED EUROPEAN RECORD, BRITISH TEAM TO APPEAL.

text.p: Britain's Susan Rolph equalled a European best time in the 200 metres individual medley on Sunday but her achievement was marked by controversy when she was denied the title of European record holder.

The organisers of the competition initially proclaimed Rolph's time of two minutes 10.60 seconds a record. It matched the mark set by East German Petra Schneider in Gainesville, Florida, in January 1982.

But the rule book does not recognise European times set in those days as official records, calling them "standard times," but still states that Schneider's time must be bettered by at least one-hundredth of a second for a record to be set.
British team manager Barbara Lancaster said she would appeal against the decision.
Rolph, who won gold in the 100 individual medley on Saturday, also missed out on prize money of 5,000 marks ($3,420) because she did not set a record.
But Lancaster said it was the record which really mattered. A British woman has not broken a European record for 10 years.
"It's not the money. She wants her name in the record book," Lancaster said.
To add insult to injury Rolph was awarded the prize of a leather jacket for best female performer at the championships in what the organisers said was a sympathy vote.
German Sandra Voelker, with five gold medals and two European records, clearly out-performed the British swimmer.
"I've stolen this jacket from you," Rolph said to Voelker. "I bought a leather jacket before I came here and I don't want another one."
Voelker said she did not understand why the performance award had gone to Rolph who had twice come second to her in both the 50 and 100 freestyle.
But Voelker thought her rival should have been awarded the European 200 medley record. "It's very German that they stick to the rules like that," she said.

Despite the disappointment of missing the record, Rolph was clearly delighted with her performance. "I looked back and I saw the clock but I could not believe it until I saw everyone jumping up and down."

"I would never have dreamed of winning two titles here and improving my best time in the 200 medley by two seconds," Rolph said. "I really feel so happy about my training, in fact I am happy about everything."
Rolph, who is studying sports science in Newcastle, northern England, said she would be heading to the local Christmas funfair with her team mates to celebrate.
